newsitem.title: CHILE: RTRS-Escondida cathode plant almost up to speed.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Escondida cathode plant almost up to speed.

text.p: Chile's Escondida copper mine has solved technical glitches at its Coloso cathodes plant which should soon be operating close to design capacity, over two years after start-up, said president Ken Pickering.
"We've been going through a shakeout in all the corners of the place and I think we're running at about 65,000 tonnes a year rate," Pickering told Reuters in an interview.
The plant, which lies on the Pacific coast south of Antofagasta, should produce at least 70,000 tonnes of cathodes during Escondida's next fiscal year, he said.
It produced 49,000 tonnes last year and is designed to churn out an annual 80,000 tonnes when working at full tilt.
The plant, which cost $200 million to build, has been plagued with technical problems since the start.
It is the first in the world to leach copper straight from concentrates using ammonia acid.
"Being a unique process, it has been a little more challenging than our engineers first throught," he said.
"The ammonia, acid and sea environment have meant that the corrosion has been incredible."
Escondida, already the world's largest concentrate producer, will become a major cathode supplier when its new oxide ore plant comes into full production around 2000.
The plant will produce 125,000 tonnes a year, bringing the company's annual cathode output to close to 200,000 tonnes.
Escondida hopes to start building work on the oxides project by mid-year, once the company receives environmental permits from the regional environment authorities, said Pickering.
The plant will cost $470 million to build -- less than usual for a scheme of this kind as it uses existing infrastructure including roads and power lines, he said.
"Grassroots projects like this somewhere by itself, without the supporting infrastructure...wouldn't fly," said Pickering.
Once the oxides plant comes into operation, Escondida's total production will rise to 900,000 - 950,000 tonnes where it will remain stable "for some time to come," he said.
Other company officials have said production could soar to 1.4 million tonnes by 2001, once the oxide plants and other projects are brought on stream.
But Pickering denied this. "It is not our intention. We must husband our resources carefully and bring things on when it makes most economic sense."
The company is carrying out exploration at the nearby Escondida Norte sulphides deposit, but has no immediate plans to develop the ore body, he said.
Escondida finished its most recent expansion, phase three, last year which allowed it to overtake the nearby state-owned Chuquicamata mine as the world's largest copper pit.
Owned by Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ-CRA the pit produced over 840,000 tonnes of copper last year.
